prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints tied to asset values amplify and propagate shocks, giving a dynamic theory of credit cycles.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part for Kiyotaki and Moore (B007). The round-1 exchange sharpened my reasons without moving my choice. The discovery is a single, identifiable mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. About three decades of theory, quantitative work and post-2008 policy analysis have put the mechanism through a real maturity test. It is also the organising device for much of the later work on financial frictions, intermediary balance sheets and macroprudential policy. The chair asked whether Kiyotaki-Moore is distinct from the 2022 prize. I think it is. That prize concerned bank runs, deposit insurance and the role of bank failures in the Great Depression. Kiyotaki-Moore needs no run and no intermediary failure. It is a general-equilibrium feedback between collateral values and credit among productive borrowers. A citation that says this explicitly would keep the discovery apart from the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator, and I would keep it to the pair for that reason. The same logic applies when I compare candidates. A crisp discovery, clear credit, durable influence and time for confirmation are the criteria, and I try not to let attribution cleanliness stand in for importance. B012 may have the larger policy footprint, and I do not claim B007 dominates it on scientific weight. I prefer B007 because the credit is clean and the contribution is a mechanism with a long record. The same reasoning leaves B026 as a close second for me.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2022 prize remains the strongest reservation. A committee that sees financial frictions as already recognised could reasonably treat Kiyotaki-Moore as a refinement, and my distinctness argument is a judgement that cannot be settled from the record alone. Second, the empirical identification of collateral channels is weaker than the theory, and the mechanism's influence runs mostly through how economists reason and build quantitative models, not through a decisive test. Several colleagues (Friberg, Hjalmarsson, Dreber-Almenberg, Strömberg) press this point and I concede it. Third, the pair leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose accelerator and intermediary work was influential, and a committee that wants a broader macro-finance award would find this prize too narrow. Fourth, B007 is a narrower body of work than the New Keynesian framework or the heterogeneous-firm framework, and I cannot rule out that I underweight breadth. My own proximity to growth and firm-dynamics research, where credit constraints matter, may make the mechanism look more general to me than it is.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers a two-part prize: Kiyotaki and Moore (B007) plus Melitz alone (B026). He admits the one-person B026 part may look like a product of the three-laureate cap and says he would prefer to name Helpman. He also says he would support Melitz and Helpman if B026 stood alone.
responses.response: I appreciate that this tests whether B007 and B026 supporters can converge. I do not adopt it. A Melitz-only part credits one person for a discovery whose two-name credit the Committee has not settled, and Helpman's place cannot be added under the three-person cap without dropping a B007 name. I do not want the cap to make the attribution decision for us. Combining a macro-finance mechanism with a trade framework also does not improve either case on merit, and it adds a cut that nobody argued for on scientific grounds. If the Committee chooses B026 as a single part, I would support Melitz and Helpman, and I note that you agree. My own remaining doubt about that pair is whether Helpman, rather than a Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributor, is the right second name. That doubt keeps B026 an alternative rather than my preferred part.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B012 first and B007 as an alternative. He places B007 below B012 because of its closeness to the 2022 prize and because the empirical support for the collateral channel is mixed. He also raises a scientific reservation that micro price data point to state-dependent adjustment, which qualifies Calvo's time-dependent mechanism.
responses.response: I agree that the empirical support for the collateral channel is mixed, and I do not claim that any single test confirms it. On the 2022 overlap I disagree, for the reasons in my case. The mechanism does not need runs or intermediary failure. Your own point about Calvo bears on the comparison, though. If micro price data challenge time-dependence, the Calvo contribution rests on an assumption of convenience rather than a confirmed mechanism, and that is a weakness in the trio. It would not remove Calvo's claim, since the assumption became the building block of the framework. It does mean B012 carries an empirical qualification of its own. In both cases the influence is on how the field reasons, so I would not penalise B007 for it more than B012. B012's breadth of institutional influence is a real advantage that I do not dispute, and I have not found a way to resolve the choice between a larger but more diffusely credited framework and a narrower mechanism with clean credit.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B012 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and B007 second. He agrees the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is the cleaner two-author discovery. He concedes that B007 and B026 have cleaner attribution than his first choice, which he calls a real argument against his own.
responses.response: Thank you for stating the attribution weakness against your own first choice. It is the main reason I hold B007 above B012. I would add that I do not treat clean attribution as evidence of merit by itself. The question I ask is whether B012's larger footprint outweighs its diffuse credit, and my answer is that a three-person cut which omits Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum or Smets leaves a gap the Committee would have to defend in public. If the Committee settles on the originators of the pricing, contracting and policy-synthesis elements, as you propose, I would regard that as a serious prize and would rank it with B026 among my alternatives. I record that you and I are co-authors. This does not enter my judgement, and you rank B007 second on the merits.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first. He moved in round 1 from a three-name proposal with Gertler to the Kiyotaki-Moore pair, citing the accelerator's entanglement with Bernanke's 2022 recognition. He argues that Gertler's claims could be judged separately, including under B012.
responses.response: I appreciate the move to the pair. We are close co-authors and now hold the same configuration, and the Committee should not count that agreement as independent confirmation. What I take from your revision is that the narrower attribution became easier to defend once Gertler's overlap with the 2022 recognition and with B012 was set aside, and that is an argument about the discovery and not a counting argument. I agree that the pair should not be read as a dismissal of Gertler's record. I would keep the citation worded around the collateral mechanism so that it leaves his work open to separate judgement. If the Committee prefers a deliberately wider macro-finance award, I would treat adding Gertler as a distinct decision. Gilchrist would then need to be considered as well, and under the three-person cap that would crowd out the clean attribution that motivates B007.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as covering the collateral-amplification mechanism, or as ground distinct enough that Kiyotaki-Moore is a separate discovery.
How to weigh the cleaner attribution and long record of B007 against the larger policy footprint of B012, given that I do not count attribution cleanliness as merit.
How much the weaker empirical identification of collateral channels should count against a mechanism whose influence runs mainly through theory and quantitative models.
Whether Helpman or a Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributor is the right second name beside Melitz, which determines how strongly I would rank B026 against B007.

Whether a deliberately wider macro-finance award adding Gertler (and Gilchrist) would be better than the pair, once the overlap with Bernanke's work is weighed. I have not independently verified citation or priority details.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Kiyotaki or Moore, the credited candidates in my preferred part, is apparent from my profile. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and a colleague of both at the IIES. Neither is a candidate, but Krusell prefers B007 and Hassler ranks B007 second, so I flag that my views overlap with theirs and that this should not be read as independent agreement. My long-running collaboration with Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li concerns work not on this shortlist. My proximity to growth and firm-dynamics research may bias my sense of B026's relevance and of how widely collateral constraints matter. My CV lists co-authorship of the Swedish popular summaries of the 2024 and 2025 prizes, and the profile gives weak evidence that I helped draft the 2025 background document. I do not treat either as bearing on any shortlisted candidate. These ties are disclosed, not adjudicated.
